title: In the town
description: Name the places in a town, and say where they are.
grammar: gender and articles, and the ending -ería
grammarNote: A shop or a workshop that sells one thing ends in -ería, and it is always feminine.

explanation.summary: A town is made of places, and most of them are named after what they do. The shops that sell one kind of thing all end in -ería, which is always feminine.

sections.heading: The places
sections.body: La iglesia, la escuela, la panadería, la farmacia, la peluquería, la biblioteca and la joyería are feminine. El ayuntamiento, el hospital and el polideportivo are masculine. The -ería ending is the clue: la panadería sells bread, la peluquería cuts hair, la farmacia sells medicine.

sections.heading: Where they are
sections.body: You already know how to say where a place is: the verb estar, then en and the place. La farmacia está en la calle mayor means the pharmacy is on the main street. En la plaza is where the town keeps its square, and the square is usually where the shops are.

examples.es: el hospital está cerca del parque
examples.en: the hospital is near the park

examples.es: la escuela está en mi barrio
examples.en: the school is in my neighbourhood

examples.es: el ayuntamiento está en la plaza
examples.en: the town hall is on the square

items.note: Masculine: el hospital. The accent marks the stress.
Feminine: la panadería. A shop that sells bread ends in -ería.
Masculine: el polideportivo. It is where people play sport indoors.
Feminine: la joyería. It sells jewellery.

drills.meaning: the bakery is on the street
the hospital is in the centre
the bakery sells bread and buns
drills.note: A shop that sells one thing ends in -ería.
